findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Restarting an unhealthy flusher in thread mode (produce_to_pipe set) leaks the hung thread, because process.kill() is skipped for non-multiprocessing.Process objects while a replacement thread is started on the same shards. In the produce_to_pipe path, a 'hang'-detected flusher thread keeps running alongside its replacement on identical shards, so segments can be read and produced by both threads (duplicate span payloads to Kafka) and thread count grows with each restart; whoever runs the consumer in pipe mode during a Redis stall gets bitten.

[ADVISORY] The two timers in the same flush cycle use inconsistent tag keys: "spans.buffer.flusher.produce" and "spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy"/"segment_size_bytes" use tag "shard" while "spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce" uses tag "shards". Anyone building dashboards or alerts grouped by shard on the flusher metrics gets wait_produce split into a differently-keyed series than the rest of the pipeline; the mismatch surfaces the first time someone aggregates produce+wait_produce per shard and gets empty joins.

[ADVISORY] Each process group constructs its own SpansBuffer(shards) instance in the parent, replacing the single shared buffer the factory created, multiplying Redis client/connection objects by num_processes. Operators raising --flusher-processes to the shard count multiply the consumer's Redis connections (one cluster client set per SpansBuffer) plus the factory's original buffer, increasing Redis connection pressure and COGS; the cost shows up as soon as flusher_processes is scaled up.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code: nothing in the diff or existing call sites invokes it, and it shadows the near-identical _create_process_for_shards. The next maintainer changing restart logic must reason about two same-shaped methods with one-letter-different names and cannot tell which is live; the confusion risk lands on whoever next edits the restart path.

[ADVISORY] The guard `if not process: continue` is dead logic: multiprocessing.Process and threading.Thread objects are always truthy, so a crashed/None-never case cannot occur and the intended early-exit never fires. Readers of the health-check loop assume there is a state where a process slot is skipped, which is false; the misleading branch costs the next debugger time when reasoning about health-check coverage.

[ADVISORY] The comment "# Check if any shard handled by this process is unhealthy" above the single healthy_since comparison is wrong: per-shard health is never checked, only the process-level healthy_since value is compared. On-call engineers investigating a hang alert will follow the comment toward per-shard health data that does not exist, wasting triage time during an incident.

[ADVISORY] `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` silently treats an explicitly configured 0 as unset, so --flusher-processes 0 produces one process per shard instead of being rejected or producing no processes. An operator setting the flag to 0 (e.g., while disabling the feature or a bad template value) gets maximum process fan-out — the opposite of intent — with no error.

[ADVISORY] The metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure") now fires inside the per-process loop and raises MessageRejected on the first offending process, so only one process's backpressure event is recorded per submit call even when several are stuck. Backpressure dashboards undercount how many flusher processes are stuck, misleading capacity debugging during Redis stalls.

[ADVISORY] The new documentation example claims hasattr(x, "replace") on a `str | None` union is WRONG, but the shown code behaves identically to the isinstance version (None has no replace attribute), so the doc asserts a false rule. Contributors following CLAUDE.md learn an incorrect claim about Python semantics and will 'fix' working hasattr checks in unrelated code during reviews, wasting review cycles.

[ADVISORY] The new multiprocess logic's restart path (_ensure_processes_alive kill-and-recreate, per-process restart counting, MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError) has no test coverage in the diff; only the happy-path process count and shard distribution are tested. A regression in the restart path (e.g., the thread-leak above, or a wrong process being killed) ships unnoticed and first manifests in production as duplicate or missing span flushes after a flusher hang.

[BUG] flusher_processes <= 0 (or a consumer misconfigured with 0) silently creates zero flusher processes and drops all buffered spans. num_processes = min(0, len(shards)) == 0, so process_to_shards_map is empty, _create_processes() starts nothing, and every shard assigned to this consumer is never flushed from Redis — spans are silently lost with no error, no unhealthy metric, and no consumer restart, since _ensure_processes_alive iterates an empty dict and always reports healthy.

[BUG] join() breaks out of the whole process loop when the deadline expires, skipping terminate() for all remaining processes. During shutdown with a timeout, the first hung process exhausts the deadline, `break` exits the outer for-loop, and every subsequent spawn process is left running (daemon flag may keep it alive until interpreter teardown, racing the producer's in-flight Kafka writes) — a shutdown hang or orphaned process leak per restart.

[BUG] Restarted processes re-pickle a fresh SpansBuffer built from SpansBuffer(shards), but the restart counter is never reset when a process is healthy, so MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS is now a lifetime cap per process slot rather than per-crash-window. Same as pre-existing behavior for a single slot, but now the RuntimeError kills the whole consumer when any ONE shard-group exceeds restarts; no test in the diff exercises _ensure_processes_alive's restart or RuntimeError path at all.

[ADVISORY] Metric tag key is inconsistent across the same flush path: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use tag `shard` while `wait_produce` uses `shards`. Dashboards/alerts split the same flusher telemetry across two tag keys, so per-shard produce-vs-wait correlation silently breaks for whoever builds the health monitoring this PR's title promises.

[ADVISORY] flusher_unhealthy metric is incremented once per shard in the process's shard list, inflating the count by the number of shards sharing a process. Alert thresholds tuned on the previous per-event semantics now fire at a different rate whenever flusher_processes < shard count, misleading the on-call engineer sizing this feature.

[ADVISORY] The new test only asserts internal data-structure shape (len(processes)==2, shard count) and never verifies that spans actually flow through shared processes to the produce_to_pipe sink. A regression where a shard assigned to a shared process is never read (e.g. the SpansBuffer(shards) constructor filtering, or main() ignoring the shards argument) passes this test while silently losing data; the PR's core claim — parallel flushing preserves end-to-end delivery — has no verification anywhere in the diff (test_flusher.py only checks a backpressure value).

[ADVISORY] No verification exists for the per-process restart path (_create_process_for_shards called from _ensure_processes_alive): killing one shared process and confirming its shards resume flushing is untested, and restart re-creates a new SpansBuffer whose assigned_shards was snapshotted at construction, so shard reassignment mid-restart is not handled. The health-monitoring restart logic — the PR's headline feature — ships with zero test coverage; the existing test_flusher.py suite was written for the single-process API (flusher.process no longer exists) and only the backpressure assertion was updated.

[ADVISORY] This diff adds a Python style-guide snippet about hasattr() vs isinstance() to CLAUDE.md, which is unrelated to the span buffer multiprocess flusher enhancement. Reviewers/maintainers get an unrelated doc change bundled into this PR, obscuring the actual change set; future readers cannot trace it to any requirement of this PR.

[ADVISORY] The wait_produce metric uses tag key "shards" while the produce timer and segment_size_bytes timing use tag key "shard", splitting the same shard dimension across two tag names. Dashboards/alerts written against spans.buffer.flusher.produce{shard=X} will not match spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce{shards=X}; on-call engineers investigating slow produce on a shard cannot correlate the two series.

[ADVISORY] The per-process health-monitoring and restart logic (_ensure_processes_alive, per-process restart counters, RuntimeError on repeated crashes) is new non-trivial behavior with no test coverage anywhere in the diff. A regression in restart logic (e.g., the kill path or process_restarts accounting) would ship unverified; the PR title promises 'Health Monitoring' but no test exercises an unhealthy or crashed process, so the invariant 'a dead flusher process is detected and restarted, and the consumer is killed after MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS' is not enforced by any test.

[ADVISORY] The test relies on a fixed time.sleep(0.1) to let flusher threads process after the drift change, and additionally the whole test monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, so the sleep inside SpanFlusher.main's loop is also removed and the 0.1s window is the only synchronization. The test flakes under CI load — when the flusher thread doesn't complete within 100ms, the assertion on message contents fails intermittently, eroding trust in the suite and masking real regressions.

[ADVISORY] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() on every per-process shard buffer and aggregates get_memory_info() across all buffers, but the submit path records stored segments for shards whose flusher buffers were constructed independently — a single consumer message is now checked against N buffer objects instead of the one authoritative buffer, changing the backpressure/memory semantics without any test asserting the multi-buffer backpressure behavior. Operators tuning spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage and the backpressure option get different aggregation behavior (sum over all shard buffers including duplicate ShardLevelMemoryInfo from shared Redis) with no test pinning the new semantics; a regression here silently changes when MessageRejected is raised in production.

[ADVISORY] Metric tag key inconsistency: produce timer uses tags={"shard": shard_tag} while wait_produce timer uses tags={"shards": shard_tag} for the same value. Dashboards/alerts querying spans.buffer.flusher.produce by tag shard will not match spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce which is tagged shards — the two series for the same process never join, and anyone building a per-shard flusher dashboard gets silently split series.

[ADVISORY] The method _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code — no caller anywhere in the diff or the restart path invokes it; restarts go through _create_process_for_shards directly. The next reader assumes shard-level restart granularity exists and wires state into it, or the two similarly-named methods drift; deleting it removes a confusable pair (shard vs shards) with no behavior change.

[ADVISORY] The test's time.sleep(0.1) 'to give flusher threads time' is a no-op because the same test monkeypatches time.sleep globally to lambda _: None three lines earlier. The wait the comment promises never happens, so the test can pass without the flusher threads having observed the drift change — a stand-in guard that goes green without exercising the race it was added for; the test is also flaky-by-luck rather than deterministic.

[ADVISORY] join()'s `break` on deadline expiry exits the outer for-loop, so every process after the timed-out one never gets terminate() called, whereas the pre-diff code always terminated its process after the wait loop. On a shutdown where the first process hangs past the join timeout, remaining flusher processes are left running (only reaped because they are daemon=True); if daemon semantics ever change or a process holds a Redis connection, shutdown leaks it — and the consumer's exit path silently differs from the single-process behavior.

[ADVISORY] The memory backpressure check sums get_memory_info() across all per-shard SpansBuffer instances, but if that call returns host/service-level memory info (not shard-scoped), used and available are double-counted by a factor of num_processes. The used/available ratio is only accidentally preserved because both sides multiply by the same factor; any future buffer implementation that returns per-instance or deduplicated memory data silently shifts the backpressure threshold, and the check now issues num_processes service-memory fetches per submit() where it previously issued one.

[ADVISORY] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() once per shard-buffer per message (num_processes Redis round trips where the previous design made one), even though the per-shard buffers each only cover their own shard range. Every submitted message multiplies its Redis bookkeeping by the flusher process count; with the new --flusher-processes knob scaled up, the consumer's submit path does proportionally more Redis work for the same message volume.

[ADVISORY] max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) treats 0 as 'unlimited' rather than 'no flusher processes'. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 (a plausible intent: disable parallel flushers) gets one process per shard — the maximum fan-out — instead of either an error or a no-op, with resource usage exploding in the opposite direction of intent.

[BUG] The refactor removes `self.buffer` and instead constructs brand-new `SpansBuffer(shards)` objects inside `_create_process_for_shards`, disconnecting the flusher processes from the buffer the consumer strategy actually writes to. The ProcessSpansStrategy (unchanged in factory.py) continues writing segments into the original full `buffer` passed at construction, while each spawned flusher process polls its own freshly constructed shard-scoped `SpansBuffer` that nothing ever writes to. Result: no segments are ever flushed, all buffered spans silently accumulate in Redis until memory-percentage backpressure raises MessageRejected and the consumer stalls — total loss of the flusher's function on the default configuration, not just the new multi-process mode.

[BUG] The memory-percentage guard now aggregates `get_memory_info()` over the flusher's internal shard buffers instead of the buffer that actually holds data. Because the shard buffers are empty constructs (per the disconnected-buffer finding above), `used` is computed from buffers with no keys, so the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` protection never trips and Redis can grow unbounded — operators relying on the documented COGS/memory backstop get a silent no-op.

[ADVISORY] The default behavior silently changed from exactly one flusher process to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` processes (one per shard) with no operator-facing decision recorded. Every existing deployment of the ingest-spans consumer that does not pass `--flusher-processes` goes from 1 spawn process to N processes on upgrade (e.g., 40 partitions = 40 spawn processes per consumer instance, each spawning its own Redis connections and producers), a resource/CODES change to existing deployments that was never explicitly accepted by the operators of currently-deployed consumers.

[BUG] The `time.sleep(0.1)` added with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is a no-op because `time.sleep` was monkeypatched to `lambda _: None` at the top of the test. The test passes without ever yielding to the flusher threads, so the comment's stated purpose (letting threads observe the drifted clock) is never achieved; the assertion that follows can pass due to prior polls rather than the sleep, masking real timing dependence and giving false confidence that the new multiprocess flusher reliably observes drift within the test's run.

[ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit asserts only internal structure (`len(flusher.processes) == 2`, shard-map totals) and never sends a single message through the pipeline, so the actual new behavior — a span landing in a given shard being flushed by the process that owns that shard's SpansBuffer — is never exercised. A regression where the per-shard SpansBuffer passed to `SpanFlusher.main` reads the wrong shards (e.g. the round-robin map built with the wrong index, or `process_to_shards_map` disagreeing with the buffers actually polled) still passes this test, because nothing verifies any span flows through either process before `step.join()`.

[ADVISORY] The new per-process health-monitoring and restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive` (hang detection via `process_healthy_since`, `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` RuntimeError, per-process kill and `_create_process_for_shards` respawn) has no test that triggers any of its branches — checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py and tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py, the only test files in the diff, and neither kills a process, blocks a shard, nor advances the restart counter. The highest-risk code in the diff (killing a hung process, restarting only the process owning a shard, and the RuntimeError path that restarts the whole consumer after repeated crashes) ships with zero verification; a bug such as an off-by-one in `process_restarts` comparison or a kill that leaves a zombie while spawning a duplicate flusher for the same shards would not be caught by any test in the diff, and in production it means duplicate Kafka production or permanent loss of flushing for those shards.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code — no call site exists in the diff or in any test; `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts via `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) directly, and the leftover singular variant additionally leaks the old process reference because it overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` without killing the previous one if it were ever called. The next maintainer extending restart logic has two similarly-named methods with divergent semantics; picking the dead one introduces an unbounded process leak, and its presence makes the correct path harder to identify.

[ADVISORY] The `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` now applies to a test that spawns multiple flusher threads per the new multiprocess design, turning each thread's `if not flushed_segments: time.sleep(1); continue` idle branch into a 100%-CPU busy-spin across N processes for the test's duration. With the new default of one flusher per shard (previously a single process), the busy-spin multiplies by shard count; under CI load the spawned threads can starve the main thread that sets `stopped`, making test_basic and the new test flaky or slow rather than 'pass instantly' as the comment claims.

[BUG] join(timeout) breaks out of the per-process loop on deadline expiry and therefore never calls terminate() on any remaining flusher processes after the current one. When the first process outlives the timeout, the break skips the terminate() calls for all subsequent process indices, so those flusher processes (which hold Redis connections and may still be producing) are left running after the strategy has reported join complete; the consumer proceeds to teardown with live producers still writing to Kafka.

[BUG] The wait_produce metric uses tag key "shards" while the produce and segment_size_bytes metrics in the same loop use tag key "shard", splitting the same dimension into two tag names. Dashboards/alerts keyed on shard=<tag> will silently miss all spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce series (they carry shards=... instead), so operators tracing a shard's health get produce timings but no produce-wait timings, and the timing series fragment across two tag schemas.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard() is dead code (no call site in this diff) and, if called, spawns a second flusher for the same shards without killing or replacing the existing process or updating self.processes[process_index]. Whoever wires this up next (it looks like the intended restart entry point for a single shard) gets two processes polling the same Redis shard keys, double-producing every segment to Kafka — silent data duplication with no error; today it is also an untested, never-exercised path that rots.

[ADVISORY] max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) treats 0 as 'unset', so an operator explicitly passing --flusher-processes 0 gets len(shards) processes instead of an error or 1. A misconfigured zero (or a future caller passing 0 as an explicit value) silently spawns one process per shard — the maximum fan-out the operator was trying to avoid — with no warning, making the knob's failure mode invisible in COGS.

[ADVISORY] The memory backpressure check now sums get_memory_info() across one SpansBuffer per process, and each of those buffers queries the same Redis service, so used/available are counted once per process for identical services. With N flusher processes, the same Redis node's ServiceMemory entries appear N times in the sum; the ratio is only accidentally preserved when all processes share identical service lists — any divergence in returned services (e.g., one buffer returning a partial list during a transient lookup failure) skews the backpressure decision, and each additional process multiplies the number of Redis memory-info lookups per submit() call.

[ADVISORY] submit() calls record_stored_segments() on every per-process SpansBuffer even though each message only pertains to one shard's buffer, and on process restart the old buffer is replaced by a freshly constructed one while old per-shard bookkeeping state lives in the discarded instance. Every submit does N redundant Redis round-trips (one per process buffer) where the single-buffer version did one, multiplying Redis load by flusher-process count on the consumer hot path; any in-memory state carried by a replaced SpansBuffer on restart is silently discarded and rebuilt from defaults.

This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, when a flusher is unhealthy it always restarts via `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`, but it only attempts to stop the old worker with `process.kill()` if `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` (thread mode uses `threading.Thread` when `produce_to_pipe` is set in `_create_process_for_shards`). There is no other mechanism shown to stop or signal the old thread on restart (the `stopped` flag is not set during restart, only in `join()`), so a hang-detected thread in pipe mode will remain alive while a replacement thread is started for the same `shards`, risking duplicate flushing/producing and unbounded thread growth across repeated restarts.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes SpanFlusher to create a separate `SpansBuffer(shards)` per process group in the parent (`_create_process_for_shards`), storing them in `self.buffers`, instead of using the single `buffer` passed into `SpanFlusher` (the previous `self.buffer = buffer` is removed). This does verifiably multiply `SpansBuffer` instances as `flusher_processes` increases. While the diff doesn’t show `SpansBuffer`’s internals, if it owns Redis clients/connections (as the finding claims), this change would scale connection usage with `num_processes` and is a concrete operational/COGS concern introduced by the change rather than a direct correctness bug.

The next maintainer changing restart logic must reason about two same-shaped methods with one-letter-different names and cannot tell which is live; the confusion risk lands on whoever next edits the restart path.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`, the diff introduces `def _create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int):` but there are no call sites shown in the diff that invoke it. The restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts via `self._create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`, and initial startup uses `_create_processes()` / `_create_process_for_shards(...)`. Having two similarly named, similarly purposed helpers (`_create_process_for_shards` vs `_create_process_for_shard`) with one apparently unused is a concrete maintainability/confusion risk grounded in this diff, but not a functional defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The guard `if not process: continue` is dead logic: multiprocessing.Process and threading.Thread objects are always truthy, so a crashed/None-never case cannot occur and the intended early-exit never fires. Readers of the health-check loop assume there is a state where a process slot is skipped, which is false; the misleading branch costs the next debugger time when reasoning about health-check coverage.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, the loop includes `if not process: continue` while `self.processes` is populated only with `process` objects created in `_create_process_for_shards` (`process.start(); self.processes[process_index] = process`). Nothing in the diff ever inserts `None` or another falsy value into `self.processes`, and `multiprocessing.Process` / `threading.Thread` instances are truthy, so the branch is effectively dead/misleading rather than fixing a real runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The comment "# Check if any shard handled by this process is unhealthy" above the single healthy_since comparison is wrong: per-shard health is never checked, only the process-level healthy_since value is compared. On-call engineers investigating a hang alert will follow the comment toward per-shard health data that does not exist, wasting triage time during an incident.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, the code determines a hang by comparing `int(time.time()) - self.process_healthy_since[process_index].value > max_unhealthy_seconds`, which is a single health timestamp per process. There is no per-shard health tracking/check beyond reporting metrics per shard after a process is deemed unhealthy. Therefore the comment `# Check if any shard handled by this process is unhealthy` is misleading relative to the implemented logic and could misdirect operational debugging, but it does not change runtime behavior (not a correctness bug).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` silently treats an explicitly configured 0 as unset, so --flusher-processes 0 produces one process per shard instead of being rejected or producing no processes. An operator setting the flag to 0 (e.g., while disabling the feature or a bad template value) gets maximum process fan-out — the opposite of intent — with no error.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__` the diff sets `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. Because `0` is falsy, an explicitly provided `max_processes=0` (possible via the new `--flusher-processes` `click.Option(type=int)` which has no min/validation) will be treated as “unset” and replaced with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, leading to `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))` becoming one process per shard. This is the opposite of what an operator likely intended when setting 0 and happens silently with no error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure") now fires inside the per-process loop and raises MessageRejected on the first offending process, so only one process's backpressure event is recorded per submit call even when several are stuck. Backpressure dashboards undercount how many flusher processes are stuck, misleading capacity debugging during Redis stalls.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.submit`, backpressure detection now iterates per-process (`for backpressure_since in self.process_backpressure_since.values():`), but it immediately does `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure")` and then `raise MessageRejected()` on the first offending process (see the loop added around lines ~264-276). This means a single `submit()` call can record at most one backpressure metric event even if multiple flusher processes are simultaneously past the threshold. That’s not a functional correctness defect (the consumer still correctly rejects), but it is a diff-grounded observability/capacity-debugging concern introduced by the new multi-process design.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new documentation example claims hasattr(x, "replace") on a `str | None` union is WRONG, but the shown code behaves identically to the isinstance version (None has no replace attribute), so the doc asserts a false rule. Contributors following CLAUDE.md learn an incorrect claim about Python semantics and will 'fix' working hasattr checks in unrelated code during reviews, wasting review cycles.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a CLAUDE.md guidance block labeling `hasattr(x, "replace")` on `x: str | None` as “WRONG” and `isinstance(x, str)` as “RIGHT”. From the shown example, both conditions behave the same at runtime (None lacks `.replace`), so the doc’s strong “WRONG” framing can be misleading/overstated based solely on the example provided. This is a documentation/review-guideline accuracy issue rather than a functional defect in the code changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new multiprocess logic's restart path (_ensure_processes_alive kill-and-recreate, per-process restart counting, MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError) has no test coverage in the diff; only the happy-path process count and shard distribution are tested. A regression in the restart path (e.g., the thread-leak above, or a wrong process being killed) ships unnoticed and first manifests in production as duplicate or missing span flushes after a flusher hang.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds nontrivial restart/health logic in `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive()` (per-process `is_alive()`/hang detection, `process_restarts` counting, `kill()` and `_create_process_for_shards()` recreation, and `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` RuntimeError). The new tests only cover the happy path: `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts process count/shard distribution, and `test_flusher` only checks backpressure flags now stored in `process_backpressure_since`. There is no test that simulates a dead/hung process/thread and verifies the correct process is killed/recreated and restart counts/error behavior, so regressions in this new restart path could ship undetected.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] flusher_processes <= 0 (or a consumer misconfigured with 0) silently creates zero flusher processes and drops all buffered spans. num_processes = min(0, len(shards)) == 0, so process_to_shards_map is empty, _create_processes() starts nothing, and every shard assigned to this consumer is never flushed from Redis — spans are silently lost with no error, no unhealthy metric, and no consumer restart, since _ensure_processes_alive iterates an empty dict and always reports healthy.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` means `max_processes=0` does **not** result in zero processes; it falls back to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. Also, even if a negative value were passed (truthy), `num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))` would be negative and the subsequent `process_index = i % self.num_processes` with `process_to_shards_map` built from `range(self.num_processes)` would likely raise (e.g., `KeyError`), not silently run with zero processes and drop spans. The described “empty dict healthy” path is not verifiable for `0` from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] join() breaks out of the whole process loop when the deadline expires, skipping terminate() for all remaining processes. During shutdown with a timeout, the first hung process exhausts the deadline, `break` exits the outer for-loop, and every subsequent spawn process is left running (daemon flag may keep it alive until interpreter teardown, racing the producer's in-flight Kafka writes) — a shutdown hang or orphaned process leak per restart.
matched_golden_ids: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate describes that when the deadline expires, the code breaks out of the loop and skips calling terminate() on remaining processes, leaving them running after shutdown—same underlying issue as the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Restarted processes re-pickle a fresh SpansBuffer built from SpansBuffer(shards), but the restart counter is never reset when a process is healthy, so MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS is now a lifetime cap per process slot rather than per-crash-window. Same as pre-existing behavior for a single slot, but now the RuntimeError kills the whole consumer when any ONE shard-group exceeds restarts; no test in the diff exercises _ensure_processes_alive's restart or RuntimeError path at all.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that restart counters are monotonic: `self.process_restarts[process_index]` is only incremented in `_ensure_processes_alive` and never reset when a process is healthy, so `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` becomes a lifetime cap per process slot (previously `self.process_restarts` in the single-process version also never reset). With multiple shard-groups, `raise RuntimeError(...)` can now be triggered by any one slot exceeding the cap, which is a behavioral/scoping concern but not a clearly verifiable correctness defect from the diff alone. The added tests (`test_flusher_processes_limit`) only cover process count/shard distribution and do not exercise the restart/RuntimeError paths in `_ensure_processes_alive`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Metric tag key is inconsistent across the same flush path: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use tag `shard` while `wait_produce` uses `shards`. Dashboards/alerts split the same flusher telemetry across two tag keys, so per-shard produce-vs-wait correlation silently breaks for whoever builds the health monitoring this PR's title promises.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`, the same flush loop emits related metrics with inconsistent tag keys: `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` and `metrics.timing("spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes", ..., tags={"shard": shard_tag})` use `shard`, while `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})` uses `shards`. This will split/fragment telemetry dimensions and hinder per-shard correlation in dashboards/alerts, but it’s an observability issue rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] flusher_unhealthy metric is incremented once per shard in the process's shard list, inflating the count by the number of shards sharing a process. Alert thresholds tuned on the previous per-event semantics now fire at a different rate whenever flusher_processes < shard count, misleading the on-call engineer sizing this feature.

adjudication.rationale:
In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, when a process is unhealthy, the code now increments `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` once **per shard** handled by that process:

```py
for shard in shards:
    metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy", tags={"cause": cause, "shard": shard})
```

Previously, the unhealthy metric was incremented once per unhealthy flusher (single process) without iterating shards. With the new shard-to-process mapping (when `flusher_processes < len(buffer.assigned_shards)`), a single unhealthy process will emit N increments (N = shards assigned), changing the metric’s rate/semantics and potentially impacting existing alert thresholds. This is an observability/alerting semantics change rather than a correctness defect in processing logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new test only asserts internal data-structure shape (len(processes)==2, shard count) and never verifies that spans actually flow through shared processes to the produce_to_pipe sink. A regression where a shard assigned to a shared process is never read (e.g. the SpansBuffer(shards) constructor filtering, or main() ignoring the shards argument) passes this test while silently losing data; the PR's core claim — parallel flushing preserves end-to-end delivery — has no verification anywhere in the diff (test_flusher.py only checks a backpressure value).

adjudication.rationale: Grounded in the diff: the newly added test `test_flusher_processes_limit` (tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py) only asserts internal bookkeeping (`len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes/num_processes == 2`, and that `process_to_shards_map` covers 4 shards). It never exercises the flusher loop to confirm that shards handled by a shared process actually flush and reach `produce_to_pipe=messages.append`. Given the refactor in `SpanFlusher` to create per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` and to pass a `shards` argument into `main()`, a regression where those shards are not actually read/produced would still pass this test. This is a specific, diff-created gap in coverage rather than a directly verifiable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No verification exists for the per-process restart path (_create_process_for_shards called from _ensure_processes_alive): killing one shared process and confirming its shards resume flushing is untested, and restart re-creates a new SpansBuffer whose assigned_shards was snapshotted at construction, so shard reassignment mid-restart is not handled. The health-monitoring restart logic — the PR's headline feature — ships with zero test coverage; the existing test_flusher.py suite was written for the single-process API (flusher.process no longer exists) and only the backpressure assertion was updated.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces nontrivial restart/health logic in `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive()` that kills and recreates a per-shard-group worker via `_create_process_for_shards()` (including new per-process `healthy_since`, `backpressure_since`, `process_restarts`, and rebuilding a `SpansBuffer(shards)` each time). The updated/new tests (`test_basic`, `test_flusher_processes_limit`, and the backpressure assertion change in `test_flusher.py`) only validate basic flushing, process-count limiting, and that backpressure exists, but they do not exercise the restart path (e.g., force a worker to die/hang and assert it is recreated and resumes flushing for its shards). The shard-reassignment concern is speculative, but the lack of coverage for the new restart mechanism is directly grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] This diff adds a Python style-guide snippet about hasattr() vs isinstance() to CLAUDE.md, which is unrelated to the span buffer multiprocess flusher enhancement. Reviewers/maintainers get an unrelated doc change bundled into this PR, obscuring the actual change set; future readers cannot trace it to any requirement of this PR.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an unrelated documentation/style-guide example to CLAUDE.md ("WRONG: Use hasattr() for unions" / "RIGHT: Use isinstance()") while the rest of the PR changes span consumer/flusher multiprocessing behavior and related tests. This bundles an orthogonal doc change into a functional PR, which can obscure review and makes the doc addition hard to trace to the PR’s purpose. It’s a real, diff-grounded scope/maintainability concern but not a runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The wait_produce metric uses tag key "shards" while the produce timer and segment_size_bytes timing use tag key "shard", splitting the same shard dimension across two tag names. Dashboards/alerts written against spans.buffer.flusher.produce{shard=X} will not match spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce{shards=X}; on-call engineers investigating slow produce on a shard cannot correlate the two series.
matched_golden_ids: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same inconsistency in metric tag keys within SpanFlusher flush metrics: using "shard" for produce/segment_size_bytes but "shards" for wait_produce, causing fragmented metric aggregation and mismatched dashboard/alert filters.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The per-process health-monitoring and restart logic (_ensure_processes_alive, per-process restart counters, RuntimeError on repeated crashes) is new non-trivial behavior with no test coverage anywhere in the diff. A regression in restart logic (e.g., the kill path or process_restarts accounting) would ship unverified; the PR title promises 'Health Monitoring' but no test exercises an unhealthy or crashed process, so the invariant 'a dead flusher process is detected and restarted, and the consumer is killed after MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS' is not enforced by any test.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new non-trivial health monitoring/restart behavior in `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive` (per-process `process_healthy_since`, `process_restarts`, kill/recreate in `_create_process_for_shards`, and `RuntimeError` after `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`). The only new tests (`test_flusher_processes_limit` and updated assertions in `test_flusher`) validate process count/shard mapping and backpressure flags, but do not exercise a dead/hung process, the kill path (`process.kill()`), restart counter increments, or the crash-loop `RuntimeError`. So the finding about missing test coverage for this new logic is grounded in the diff and is actionable, but it’s not itself a verified defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test relies on a fixed time.sleep(0.1) to let flusher threads process after the drift change, and additionally the whole test monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, so the sleep inside SpanFlusher.main's loop is also removed and the 0.1s window is the only synchronization. The test flakes under CI load — when the flusher thread doesn't complete within 100ms, the assertion on message contents fails intermittently, eroding trust in the suite and masking real regressions.

[ADVISORY] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() on every per-process shard buffer and aggregates get_memory_info() across all buffers, but the submit path records stored segments for shards whose flusher buffers were constructed independently — a single consumer message is now checked against N buffer objects instead of the one authoritative buffer, changing the backpressure/memory semantics without any test asserting the multi-buffer backpressure behavior. Operators tuning spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage and the backpressure option get different aggregation behavior (sum over all shard buffers including duplicate ShardLevelMemoryInfo from shared Redis) with no test pinning the new semantics; a regression here silently changes when MessageRejected is raised in production.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly changes semantics in `SpanFlusher.submit()`: it now iterates over `self.buffers.values()` to call `record_stored_segments()` and aggregates memory via `memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` (previously a single `self.buffer`). It also rejects if *any* `process_backpressure_since` exceeds the threshold, rather than a single backpressure flag. However, the finding’s claims about “duplicate ShardLevelMemoryInfo from shared Redis” and the exact operator-facing aggregation effects aren’t verifiable from this diff because `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` isn’t shown. What *is* grounded is that these nontrivial semantic changes are not covered by tests (new tests only assert process-count/shard distribution and a backpressure assertion was loosened to `any(...)`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Metric tag key inconsistency: produce timer uses tags={"shard": shard_tag} while wait_produce timer uses tags={"shards": shard_tag} for the same value. Dashboards/alerts querying spans.buffer.flusher.produce by tag shard will not match spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce which is tagged shards — the two series for the same process never join, and anyone building a per-shard flusher dashboard gets silently split series.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`, the diff introduces inconsistent metric tag keys for the same shard identifier: `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` vs `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})`. This will split metric series and make per-shard dashboards/alerts harder or incorrect, but it does not break runtime behavior of flushing itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The method _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code — no caller anywhere in the diff or the restart path invokes it; restarts go through _create_process_for_shards directly. The next reader assumes shard-level restart granularity exists and wires state into it, or the two similarly-named methods drift; deleting it removes a confusable pair (shard vs shards) with no behavior change.

adjudication.rationale: In src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py the new helper `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is added but nothing in the diff calls it. The restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive()` directly calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`, and initialization uses `_create_processes()` -> `_create_process_for_shards(...)`. With no references shown, `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code and creates a confusing near-duplicate API (shard vs shards) without affecting behavior if removed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test's time.sleep(0.1) 'to give flusher threads time' is a no-op because the same test monkeypatches time.sleep globally to lambda _: None three lines earlier. The wait the comment promises never happens, so the test can pass without the flusher threads having observed the drift change — a stand-in guard that goes green without exercising the race it was added for; the test is also flaky-by-luck rather than deterministic.
matched_golden_ids: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate points out that the test monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op (lambda _: None) and then later calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting a real delay, meaning the intended wait never occurs. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] join()'s `break` on deadline expiry exits the outer for-loop, so every process after the timed-out one never gets terminate() called, whereas the pre-diff code always terminated its process after the wait loop. On a shutdown where the first process hangs past the join timeout, remaining flusher processes are left running (only reaped because they are daemon=True); if daemon semantics ever change or a process holds a Redis connection, shutdown leaks it — and the consumer's exit path silently differs from the single-process behavior.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.join()`, the new loop over `self.processes` does `if remaining_time <= 0: break`, which exits the *outer* `for` loop (not just the per-process wait). That means any processes after the one that consumed the deadline will not reach the subsequent `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.terminate()` block. Pre-diff, the single process was always terminated after the wait loop regardless of deadline expiry. This diff therefore introduces a real shutdown-behavior change where some flusher processes may be left running past `join()`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The memory backpressure check sums get_memory_info() across all per-shard SpansBuffer instances, but if that call returns host/service-level memory info (not shard-scoped), used and available are double-counted by a factor of num_processes. The used/available ratio is only accidentally preserved because both sides multiply by the same factor; any future buffer implementation that returns per-instance or deduplicated memory data silently shifts the backpressure threshold, and the check now issues num_processes service-memory fetches per submit() where it previously issued one.

adjudication.rationale: In SpanFlusher.submit(), the memory backpressure check changed from a single `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` call to iterating all per-process buffers and `extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` (see `memory_infos: list[ServiceMemory] = []` loop). This is a concrete behavioral/perf change: it now performs `num_processes` memory-info fetches per submit(), and if `get_memory_info()` returns service/host-level (non-shard-scoped) data, the totals (`used`/`available`) will be duplicated across buffers. While the ratio may remain the same if both numerator and denominator scale equally, the duplication and extra calls are real diff-grounded concerns and could affect thresholds if the underlying implementation changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() once per shard-buffer per message (num_processes Redis round trips where the previous design made one), even though the per-shard buffers each only cover their own shard range. Every submitted message multiplies its Redis bookkeeping by the flusher process count; with the new --flusher-processes knob scaled up, the consumer's submit path does proportionally more Redis work for the same message volume.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `SpanFlusher.submit()` from a single `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()` call to iterating all per-process buffers: `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()` (flusher.py). Since `self.buffers` is sized to `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`, this makes the submit path do work proportional to the configured flusher process count. Whether this is strictly “num_processes Redis round trips” depends on `record_stored_segments()` internals (not shown), but the added per-message loop across buffers is real and is a concrete performance/architecture concern introduced by the change, not a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) treats 0 as 'unlimited' rather than 'no flusher processes'. An operator setting --flusher-processes 0 (a plausible intent: disable parallel flushers) gets one process per shard — the maximum fan-out — instead of either an error or a no-op, with resource usage exploding in the opposite direction of intent.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` will treat an explicit `max_processes=0` as falsy and replace it with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. The new CLI option `--flusher-processes` is `type=int` and can accept `0`, and `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory` passes it through (`max_processes=self.flusher_processes`). So setting `--flusher-processes 0` would unexpectedly fan out to one process per shard (`num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))`), the opposite of the operator’s likely intent, and can increase resource usage dramatically.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The refactor removes `self.buffer` and instead constructs brand-new `SpansBuffer(shards)` objects inside `_create_process_for_shards`, disconnecting the flusher processes from the buffer the consumer strategy actually writes to. The ProcessSpansStrategy (unchanged in factory.py) continues writing segments into the original full `buffer` passed at construction, while each spawned flusher process polls its own freshly constructed shard-scoped `SpansBuffer` that nothing ever writes to. Result: no segments are ever flushed, all buffered spans silently accumulate in Redis until memory-percentage backpressure raises MessageRejected and the consumer stalls — total loss of the flusher's function on the default configuration, not just the new multi-process mode.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `SpanFlusher` no longer stores `self.buffer` and instead creates per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances in `_create_process_for_shards`. However, the finding’s claim that this *necessarily* disconnects the flusher from what the consumer writes (so nothing is ever flushed) is not verifiable from the diff: there is no evidence here that `SpansBuffer` holds unique, per-instance in-memory state that must be shared with the writer, or that constructing a new `SpansBuffer` for the same shard IDs would point at a different Redis namespace. The refactor appears intentionally to shard-scope buffers per process, and could still read the same underlying Redis data keyed by shard IDs. Thus the asserted “total loss of the flusher’s function” is not grounded in what the diff alone proves.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The memory-percentage guard now aggregates `get_memory_info()` over the flusher's internal shard buffers instead of the buffer that actually holds data. Because the shard buffers are empty constructs (per the disconnected-buffer finding above), `used` is computed from buffers with no keys, so the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` protection never trips and Redis can grow unbounded — operators relying on the documented COGS/memory backstop get a silent no-op.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the memory guard to aggregate `get_memory_info()` across `self.buffers` (new per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances) instead of a single `self.buffer`. But the diff provides no evidence that these shard buffers are “empty constructs” or disconnected from the actual Redis state; they are instantiated with the shards they’re responsible for and are the same buffers used by the flusher processes (`partial(SpanFlusher.main, shard_buffer)`). Without seeing `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()`/its linkage to Redis, the claim that `used` will be computed as zero and the guard will silently never trip is not verifiable from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The default behavior silently changed from exactly one flusher process to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` processes (one per shard) with no operator-facing decision recorded. Every existing deployment of the ingest-spans consumer that does not pass `--flusher-processes` goes from 1 spawn process to N processes on upgrade (e.g., 40 partitions = 40 spawn processes per consumer instance, each spawning its own Redis connections and producers), a resource/CODES change to existing deployments that was never explicitly accepted by the operators of currently-deployed consumers.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an operator-facing Click option `--flusher-processes` with `default=1` for the `process-spans` consumer (`src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py`), and wires it through `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory(... flusher_processes: int | None = None ...)` into `SpanFlusher(max_processes=...)` (`factory.py`). So for existing deployments using the Click/consumer entrypoint, not specifying `--flusher-processes` still results in `flusher_processes=1`, not `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. While `SpanFlusher` does default to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` when `max_processes` is `None` (`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` in `flusher.py`), the finding’s claim about “every existing deployment … that does not pass `--flusher-processes`” changing from 1 to N is not supported by the diff because the CLI default is explicitly 1.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The `time.sleep(0.1)` added with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is a no-op because `time.sleep` was monkeypatched to `lambda _: None` at the top of the test. The test passes without ever yielding to the flusher threads, so the comment's stated purpose (letting threads observe the drifted clock) is never achieved; the assertion that follows can pass due to prior polls rather than the sleep, masking real timing dependence and giving false confidence that the new multiprocess flusher reliably observes drift within the test's run.

adjudication.rationale: In `test_basic`, `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` is applied at the top of the test, and later the test calls `time.sleep(0.1)` (after an extra `step.poll()`) with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change". Because the call site uses `time.sleep` from the `time` module, that sleep is indeed patched to a no-op, so it cannot serve the stated purpose. This is a test-quality/clarity issue (misleading comment/ineffective wait) rather than a production defect in the PR’s logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit asserts only internal structure (`len(flusher.processes) == 2`, shard-map totals) and never sends a single message through the pipeline, so the actual new behavior — a span landing in a given shard being flushed by the process that owns that shard's SpansBuffer — is never exercised. A regression where the per-shard SpansBuffer passed to `SpanFlusher.main` reads the wrong shards (e.g. the round-robin map built with the wrong index, or `process_to_shards_map` disagreeing with the buffers actually polled) still passes this test, because nothing verifies any span flows through either process before `step.join()`.

adjudication.rationale: The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` only inspects internal state (`len(flusher.processes)`, `flusher.max_processes`, `flusher.num_processes`, and the summed shard counts in `process_to_shards_map`) and then calls `step.join()` without ever submitting any messages/spans or asserting any flush/produce behavior. Given the diff also introduced nontrivial shard-to-process routing and per-process `SpansBuffer` construction in `SpanFlusher.__init__` / `_create_process_for_shards` (creating `shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)` and passing it to `SpanFlusher.main`), a mismatch between `process_to_shards_map` and what buffers/processes actually poll would not be caught by this test as written. This is a specific, diff-grounded gap in test coverage rather than a directly verifiable functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new per-process health-monitoring and restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive` (hang detection via `process_healthy_since`, `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` RuntimeError, per-process kill and `_create_process_for_shards` respawn) has no test that triggers any of its branches — checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py and tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py, the only test files in the diff, and neither kills a process, blocks a shard, nor advances the restart counter. The highest-risk code in the diff (killing a hung process, restarting only the process owning a shard, and the RuntimeError path that restarts the whole consumer after repeated crashes) ships with zero verification; a bug such as an off-by-one in `process_restarts` comparison or a kill that leaves a zombie while spawning a duplicate flusher for the same shards would not be caught by any test in the diff, and in production it means duplicate Kafka production or permanent loss of flushing for those shards.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds substantial new logic in `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive` (per-process `is_alive`/hang detection via `process_healthy_since`, incrementing `process_restarts`, killing and respawning only the affected process via `_create_process_for_shards`, and raising `RuntimeError` after `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`). The added/modified tests (`test_basic`, `test_flusher_processes_limit`, and the updated `test_flusher` assertion) do not exercise any unhealthy branches: they never simulate a dead process, a hung process (e.g., stale `process_healthy_since` beyond `max-unhealthy-seconds`), nor the restart counter exceeding the limit. So the finding that these high-risk branches ship without verification is accurate and specific to the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code — no call site exists in the diff or in any test; `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts via `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) directly, and the leftover singular variant additionally leaks the old process reference because it overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` without killing the previous one if it were ever called. The next maintainer extending restart logic has two similarly-named methods with divergent semantics; picking the dead one introduces an unbounded process leak, and its presence makes the correct path harder to identify.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is introduced but has no call site shown (the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` directly calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). The singular helper also restarts by calling `_create_process_for_shards` without terminating/killing any existing process first, while `_create_process_for_shards` overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` after starting a new process/thread. This makes the method misleading/unused and creates a sharp edge for future maintainers (if they call it, it could spawn an extra process for the same shard group). It’s not a presently-triggered runtime defect based solely on the diff because it’s dead code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` now applies to a test that spawns multiple flusher threads per the new multiprocess design, turning each thread's `if not flushed_segments: time.sleep(1); continue` idle branch into a 100%-CPU busy-spin across N processes for the test's duration. With the new default of one flusher per shard (previously a single process), the busy-spin multiplies by shard count; under CI load the spawned threads can starve the main thread that sets `stopped`, making test_basic and the new test flaky or slow rather than 'pass instantly' as the comment claims.

adjudication.rationale: The diff keeps `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` in `test_basic` (and adds it to `test_flusher_processes_limit`), while `SpanFlusher.main` still has an idle path `if not flushed_segments: time.sleep(1); continue`. With the new design, `SpanFlusher.__init__` creates `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` and `_create_processes()` starts one thread per `process_index` when `produce_to_pipe` is set (tests pass `produce_to_pipe=messages.append`). That means tests now spawn multiple flusher threads (typically one per shard by default), and patching `time.sleep` to a no-op turns each thread’s idle loop into a tight busy-spin, plausibly making tests slow/flaky under CI load.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] join(timeout) breaks out of the per-process loop on deadline expiry and therefore never calls terminate() on any remaining flusher processes after the current one. When the first process outlives the timeout, the break skips the terminate() calls for all subsequent process indices, so those flusher processes (which hold Redis connections and may still be producing) are left running after the strategy has reported join complete; the consumer proceeds to teardown with live producers still writing to Kafka.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.join`, the per-process loop does `if remaining_time <= 0: break` before waiting/terminating the current `process` (for that iteration), which exits the *entire* `for process_index, process in self.processes.items()` loop. This means once the deadline is exceeded before reaching later entries, those subsequent flusher processes will not go through the `while process.is_alive()` wait nor the `process.terminate()` call at the end of the loop, and can remain running after `join()` returns.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The wait_produce metric uses tag key "shards" while the produce and segment_size_bytes metrics in the same loop use tag key "shard", splitting the same dimension into two tag names. Dashboards/alerts keyed on shard=<tag> will silently miss all spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce series (they carry shards=... instead), so operators tracing a shard's health get produce timings but no produce-wait timings, and the timing series fragment across two tag schemas.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.main` the same shard dimension is tagged inconsistently: `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` and `metrics.timing("spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes", ..., tags={"shard": shard_tag})` use tag key `shard`, but `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})` uses `shards`. This splits the metric series across two tag schemas, so shard-filtered dashboards/alerts keyed on `shard` will not include the `wait_produce` series.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard() is dead code (no call site in this diff) and, if called, spawns a second flusher for the same shards without killing or replacing the existing process or updating self.processes[process_index]. Whoever wires this up next (it looks like the intended restart entry point for a single shard) gets two processes polling the same Redis shard keys, double-producing every segment to Kafka — silent data duplication with no error; today it is also an untested, never-exercised path that rots.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `_create_process_for_shard()` is newly added in `SpanFlusher` but there is no call site shown (only `_ensure_processes_alive()` restarts via `_create_process_for_shards`). So it is currently dead/untested. The finding’s risk claim is also grounded: `_create_process_for_shard()` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` without first killing/terminating the existing `self.processes[process_index]`, and `_create_process_for_shards`/`_create_process_for_shards` always starts a new process/thread and then overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` with the new handle. That would leave the old process alive and polling the same shard set, plausibly causing duplicate production if this path were wired up later. However, since the diff shows no current usage, it’s not a verifiable present defect in behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) treats 0 as 'unset', so an operator explicitly passing --flusher-processes 0 gets len(shards) processes instead of an error or 1. A misconfigured zero (or a future caller passing 0 as an explicit value) silently spawns one process per shard — the maximum fan-out the operator was trying to avoid — with no warning, making the knob's failure mode invisible in COGS.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, the new logic sets `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. Because `0` is falsy, an explicit `flusher_processes=0` (possible via the newly added `click.Option(... type=int ...)` which has no lower-bound validation) will be treated as “unset” and will fall back to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. That directly causes `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` to become `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, i.e., maximum fan-out, which contradicts the intent of passing 0 and happens silently.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The memory backpressure check now sums get_memory_info() across one SpansBuffer per process, and each of those buffers queries the same Redis service, so used/available are counted once per process for identical services. With N flusher processes, the same Redis node's ServiceMemory entries appear N times in the sum; the ratio is only accidentally preserved when all processes share identical service lists — any divergence in returned services (e.g., one buffer returning a partial list during a transient lookup failure) skews the backpressure decision, and each additional process multiplies the number of Redis memory-info lookups per submit() call.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the memory backpressure logic in `SpanFlusher.submit()` from `list(self.buffer.get_memory_info())` to aggregating across per-process buffers: `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` (flusher.py). Since each `SpansBuffer` likely queries the same Redis service(s), this can multiply `get_memory_info()` calls per submit and can duplicate `ServiceMemory` entries in the `used`/`available` sums. While the used/available ratio would remain the same if every buffer returns the exact same service list, the finding’s concern about unnecessary repeated lookups and potential skew if buffers return differing/partial lists is a concrete, diff-grounded risk/efficiency issue rather than a clearly verifiable correctness bug from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] submit() calls record_stored_segments() on every per-process SpansBuffer even though each message only pertains to one shard's buffer, and on process restart the old buffer is replaced by a freshly constructed one while old per-shard bookkeeping state lives in the discarded instance. Every submit does N redundant Redis round-trips (one per process buffer) where the single-buffer version did one, multiplying Redis load by flusher-process count on the consumer hot path; any in-memory state carried by a replaced SpansBuffer on restart is silently discarded and rebuilt from defaults.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows SpanFlusher.submit() now iterates over all per-process buffers and calls record_stored_segments() on each: `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()` (previously a single `self.buffer.record_stored_segments()`). This is a concrete change that can multiply work on the submit path by the number of flusher processes. The diff also shows process restarts create a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` and replace `self.buffers[process_index]` in `_create_process_for_shards`, discarding the prior buffer instance. Whether this causes lost in-memory bookkeeping or extra Redis round-trips depends on SpansBuffer internals (not shown), so it's best characterized as a specific performance/architecture concern grounded in the change rather than a proven correctness bug.
